pack.title: Unit 5.0 Configuring Routing and Advanced Switching

flashcards.definition: A device with links to more than one network that forwards packets between subnets and around an internetwork; hosts in different subnets must be separated by one.
The general name for a device or host software that filters traffic by rules, blocking anything that does not conform to a rule.
The IP header field that each router lowers by at least 1, discarding the packet at 0 so it cannot circle the network forever.
Many-to-many links, with each node having multiple interfaces and cable paths to other nodes, which gives redundant paths.
Any mixture of point-to-point, star, and mesh topologies.
One-to-many links in which each node relies on a central forwarding device to reach the other nodes.
A one-to-one link between two hosts only.
A design that breaks a large network into sections by function, with separate access, distribution, and core layers.
The highly available backbone at the top of the three-tier design, giving redundant paths for traffic.
The middle layer that gives fault-tolerant links between the access blocks and the core.
The bottom layer, where end user devices such as computers and smartphones connect to the network.
A two-tier design that combines the core and distribution layers.
Routes an administrator adds to the routing table by hand; they change only when edited, so they are hard to maintain if the topology changes often.
Routers share route information with their neighbors through a protocol that uses an algorithm and metrics to choose among paths, instead of entries typed in by hand.
The protocol that routes between autonomous systems on the Internet, mainly between ISPs.
A routing protocol whose default metric is built from bandwidth and delay, and which sends updates only when the topology changes.
The link state protocol that groups routers into areas joined by a backbone and finds least-cost paths from each area's topology database.
The order a router follows when several routes match: prefix length first, then administrative distance, then metric.
A value rating how trustworthy a route's source is, used to choose between routes with equal prefixes from different protocols; the lower value wins.
The first factor in choosing among matching routes: the most specific entry, such as a /28 over a /24, is preferred.
The cost a routing protocol calculates for each path, such as hop count; the lowest cost wins, but it cannot compare routes from different protocols.
A service on a border device, such as a router, proxy server, or firewall, that converts between private LAN addresses and public ones; the static form maps them 1:1.
Lets many private addresses share one public address by giving each connection its own port number.
Logical interfaces made on one physical router interface, each with its own VLAN ID and IP address to act as that VLAN's default gateway.
A group of ports on a managed switch, set by an ID, that forms its own broadcast domain; traffic to another group must go through a router or layer 3 switch.
The record of every VLAN configured on a switch, which show vlan reports along with each VLAN's ports.
The default gateway for one VLAN on a layer 3 switch, bound to the VLAN itself rather than to a physical port.
The VLAN that a trunk port puts untagged frames into; it should be set the same on both ends of the trunk.
A separate VLAN for VoIP handsets so voice traffic can be given priority; the handset marks its voice frames with an 802.1Q tag.
The IEEE standard that inserts a VLAN ID tag into each Ethernet frame sent over a trunk, so the receiving switch can forward it to the right VLAN.
The largest IP datagram one Data Link frame can carry; usually 1,500 bytes on Ethernet.
A host connected to a port in the wrong VLAN, so it cannot reach the hosts and default gateway of the VLAN it belongs in.
Lists of rules on a firewall or router, each defining a type of packet and whether to accept or deny it.
A router's or host's list of available paths, each entry giving a destination, the interface to use, and the next hop.
The special static route, 0.0.0.0/0 in IPv4, used for any destination that no other entry matches.
Tests a path hop by hop, raising the probes' TTL by one each time, to find the node or link causing a problem; by default, Windows probes with ICMP, and Linux and routers with UDP.
The router command that displays its active routing table.
The router command that lists its cache of IP addresses resolved to MAC addresses.
The switch command that reports each configured VLAN ID and the ports assigned to it.
Accepting or denying packets by the source and destination port numbers in their TCP or UDP headers.
A firewall that tracks each session between two hosts in a state table, so it can spot attacks spread over many packets that a stateless packet filter misses.
The process by which routers running a dynamic routing protocol share changes until they all agree on the network topology.
The distance vector protocol whose only metric is hop count; it sends its entire database to its neighbors at regular intervals.
The type of routing protocol that relies on neighboring routers to report paths to remote networks; RIP is one, and it counts hops.
The type of routing protocol in which each router stores the complete network topology and calculates least-cost paths from it, not from neighbors' hop counts.
The category of routing protocol that advertises routes between autonomous systems, such as BGP; an IGP works within one.
The command that views and changes the routing table of Windows and Linux hosts; the ip command can do the same job on Linux.
A switch optimized for routing between VLANs, so it can do that job in place of a router.
VLAN 1, which every switch port is in until configured otherwise; it cannot be changed.
